questions.q: What was the main provision of the Rowlatt Act (1919) that angered Indians the most?
questions.a: The Rowlatt Act allowed the British government to imprison any person suspected of revolutionary activities without trial for up to two years, and denied the right to appeal. A wrong answer (e.g., "it increased taxes" or "it banned the Congress") reveals the student confuses the Rowlatt Act with other repressive laws like the Defence of India Act or the Press Act.

questions.q: Why did Gandhi call for a nationwide hartal (strike) on 6 April 1919 against the Rowlatt Act?
questions.a: Gandhi called for a hartal because the Rowlatt Act was passed despite unanimous opposition from Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council, violating the principle of no taxation without representation and denying basic civil liberties. A wrong answer (e.g., "because the British killed people at Jallianwala Bagh") reveals the student confuses the chronology — the hartal was *before* the massacre, not after.

questions.q: Analyze the following source: "The gathering at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919 included many villagers who had come for the Baisakhi fair and were unaware of the ban on public meetings." What does this tell us about the nature of the crowd and the British response?
questions.a: The crowd was largely unarmed, included women and children, and many were not political protesters but festival-goers. The British response — General Dyer ordering firing without warning or dispersal order — was disproportionate and aimed at creating a "moral effect" to terrorize Punjab. A wrong answer (e.g., "the crowd was violent and attacked the soldiers") reveals the student has internalized the British justification and misses the asymmetry of violence.

questions.q: Compare the British government's reaction to the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (Hunter Committee, Dyer's censure) with the Indian nationalist reaction (Rabindranath Tagore's knighthood surrender, Gandhi's loss of faith in British justice). What does this contrast reveal about the legitimacy crisis of British rule?
questions.a: The British reaction treated Dyer's action as an error of judgment by one officer, while Indians saw it as systemic racism and the true face of colonial rule. The contrast reveals that the massacre broke the moral contract — Indians no longer believed the British could be fair rulers. A wrong answer (e.g., "both sides condemned it equally") reveals the student misses the fundamental divergence: the British inquiry exonerated the policy, while Indians rejected the system.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Jallianwala Bagh Massacre was the turning point that made the Non-Cooperation Movement inevitable." Support your answer with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: Yes, it was a turning point. Evidence 1: Gandhi, who had earlier supported the British in WWI, now declared cooperation with "satanic" government impossible. Evidence 2: The Congress session at Amritsar (Dec 1919) saw a surge in delegates and the demand for purna swaraj grew louder. A wrong answer (e.g., "the massacre had no link to Non-Cooperation") reveals the student fails to connect the emotional and political rupture caused by the massacre to the launch of the first mass movement.

questions.q: Construct a timeline with four key events from March to December 1919 that shows the escalation from the Rowlatt Act to the launch of the Non-Cooperation Movement. Include dates.
questions.a: A good timeline: 1) March 1919: Rowlatt Act passed. 2) 6 April 1919: Gandhi's hartal. 3) 13 April 1919: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. 4) Oct 1919: Hunter Committee formed. 5) Dec 1919: Amritsar Congress session demands self-government; 6) 1920: Non-Cooperation launched. A poor answer (missing dates, wrong order, or omitting the hartal) reveals the student cannot sequence cause-effect in the critical months of 1919.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Rowlatt Act (1919) was a repressive ______ passed by the British Imperial Legislative Council that allowed detention of political prisoners without trial and curbed civil liberties.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are visiting the ______ Bagh memorial in Amritsar today — you see the bullet marks on the walls and the well where people jumped to escape.

Fill in the blank: The Rowlatt Act (______) was a repressive legislation passed by the British Imperial Legislative Council that allowed detention of political prisoners without trial and curbed civil liberties.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the provisions of the Rowlatt Act, analyze why it provoked nationwide protests, and evaluate the impact of the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre on the Indian nationalist movement and British legitimacy.
